messages.author: d1e9d30595320d5e
messages.subject: Problem setting up Hierarchical IRT model with 'student' and 'test' levels
parts:
I have a question that I think has a simple answer, but I can't seem to see it.

Set up: I'm building an item-response model based directly on the multilevel 2PL example from the docs. My data is in country-year format with binary variables for whether or not country j reported a given data point to the World Bank in year t. I'm primarily interested in estimating each country's 'transparency' for each year. This is equivalent to 'student's ability' in the Stan IRT example.

In the model the transparency variables are denoted with alpha.

Problem: I can easily run the model for just one year. You can fully reproduce this with rstan using code at:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/FGCH/FRTIndex/stanTest/source/FRT_Stan.R

What I'm stuck on is how to estimate alpha for each country year j,t (I guess this would be equivalent to having 'student' and 'number times the student took the test'). 

This is what I have so far:

    data {
        int<lower=1> J;                // number of countries
        int<lower=1> T;                // number of years
        int<lower=1> K;                // number of items
        int<lower=1> N;                // number of observations
        int<lower=1> jj[N];            // country for observation n
        int<lower=1> tt[N];            // time for observation n
        int<lower=1,upper=K> kk[N];    // question for observation n
        int<lower=0,upper=1> y[N];     // correctness for observation n
    }

    parameters {
        real delta;                    // mean transparency
        real alpha[J,T];               // transparency for j,t - mean
        real beta[K];                  // difficulty of item k
        real log_gamma[K];             // discrimination of k
        real<lower=0> sigma_alpha;     // scale of abilities
        real<lower=0> sigma_beta;      // scale of difficulties
        real<lower=0> sigma_gamma;     // scale of log discrimiation
    }

    model {
        alpha ~ normal(0,sigma_alpha);
        beta ~ normal(0,sigma_beta);
        log_gamma ~ normal(0,sigma_gamma);
        delta ~ cauchy(0,5);
        sigma_alpha ~ cauchy(0,5);
        sigma_beta ~ cauchy(0,5);
        sigma_gamma ~ cauchy(0,5);
        for (n in 1:N)
            y[n] ~ bernoulli_logit( exp(log_gamma[kk[n]])
                                * (alpha[jj[n],tt[n]] - beta[kk[n]] + delta) );
    }

However, using this model in stan returns the error no matches for function name="normal_log". The full replication code is available at:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/FGCH/FRTIndex/stanTest/source/FRT_Stan_v0_2.R

Any help with this would be much appreciated.

For future reference, it helps to provide the actual error message. My guess is that the error has to do with this line:
       alpha ~ normal(0,sigma_alpha);

The "no matches for function..." message probably lists a line and what arguments you provided with a list of available arguments.

The normal distribution (currently) does not accept matrix arguments, so you'll have to loop over the years or countries.

messages.author: cab04b8f0759c712
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: Problem setting up Hierarchical IRT model with 'student' and 'test' levels
parts:
Hi Chris,

The issue is:

no matches for function name="normal_log"
    arg 0 type=real[2]
    arg 1 type=int
    arg 2 type=real

For the left hand side of this expression:
alpha ~ normal(0,sigma_alpha);
you have alpha defined as:
real alpha[J,T];               // transparency for j,t - mean

If you want to use alpha as is, you'll need to replace "alpha ~ normal(0, sigma_alpha);" with:
    for (j in 1:J)
      for (t in 1:T)
        alpha[j, t] ~ normal(0, sigma_alpha);

or
    for (j in 1:J)
       alpha[j] ~ normal(0, sigma_alpha);

The second one uses the vectorized form for the left side.



So... the message is telling you that Stan doesn't have the normal distribution defined for a 2-d array of reals. We need to add better error messages, but that's how to interpret "arg 0 type=real[2]".



Daniel

> alpha ~ normal(0,sigma_alpha);
> to

> alpha ~ normal(0.0,sigma_alpha);
> may work? 0 is considered as an integer whereas 0.0 as considered as real.
>

If there's ever a place where 0.0 works but 0 doesn't,
that's a bug and we'd appreciate hearing about it.
C++ doesn't have this problem with non-templated
functions, because int can be promoted to double. Ditto
for Java and C. But in C++ templates, it's possible to
specialize so that there's a definition for double inputs
but not int inputs; and if the templates can't resolve,
no go.

The problem here, as Daniel pointed out, is that the
normal_log function doesn't accept real[2] (i.e., 2D
array of real) arguments.

I want to replace the error output "real[2]" with
"real[,]" because that's what we're using in the function
syntax and I think it'll be clearer than just reporting the
number of arguments as we currently do:

> no matches for function name="normal_log"
> arg 0 type=real[2]
> arg 1 type=int
> arg 2 type=real
- Bob

messages.author: d1e9d30595320d5e
messages.subject: Re: Problem setting up Hierarchical IRT model with 'student' and 'test' levels
parts:
Thanks! This discussion has been really useful. It's really helping me convert my IRT models to Stan from Jags (so far I've definitely had the advertised convergence speed improvements).

This worked perfectly:

for (j in 1:J)
    for (t in 1:T)
        alpha[j,t] ~ normal(0, sigma_alpha);

FYI for anyone else that might be interested: I've updated the priors slightly such that at time 1 alpha[j,t] ~ normal(0, sigma_alpha), but then for all t_1+n the previous year's alpha informs the prior for the following year, i.e.

for (j in 1:J)
    alpha[j,1] ~ normal(0, sigma_alpha);
for (j in 1:J)
    for (t in 2:T)
        alpha[j,t] ~ normal(alpha[j,t-1], sigma_alpha);

Any thoughts on further tweaks would be of course be welcome.

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: Problem setting up Hierarchical IRT model with 'student' and 'test' levels
parts:
You can probably continue to vectorize.
I'm not sure what your data types are, though.

If alpha[j,t] is a scalar, then it might help to
transpose alpha and use alpha_t[t,j], at which

point you could write:

for (t in 1:T)

alpha_t[t] ~ normal(alpha_t[t-1], sigma_alpha);

You'd also be able to write just

alpha_t[1] ~ normal(0, sigma_alpha);

Even better if you declare alpha_t as an array of vectors.
There's a chapter in the manual now on arrays versus
vectors and speed and where they are required.

This can be a really big speedup if J >> 1.

- Bob

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: Problem setting up Hierarchical IRT model with 'student' and 'test' levels
parts:
Each data structure has a dimensionality, for instance, both of

matrix[M,N] a;

vector[N] a[M];

define an (M x N) structure. To use Daniel's suggestion, you need
to read the data in transposed.

To just transpose in the model, all you need to replace the declaration

real alpha[J,T];

with

matrix[J,T] alpha;

and then define:

transformed data {
matrix[T,J] alpha_t;
alpha_t <- alpha';
}

even more efficient would be:

transformed data {
vector[J] alpha_t[T];
for (t in 1:T)

alpha_t[t] <- col(alpha,t);
}

Then just use alpha_t in the code as suggested earlier.

But I wouldn't worry about any of this if the model's fast
enough without it.

- Bob

The manual chapter explains all of that.

real[,] : std::vector<std:vector<double> >.

matrix : Eigen::Matrix<double,Eigen::Dynamic,Eigen::Dynamic>.

No copying should be needed because indexing returns a reference.

We haven't seen these 2D array vs. matrix differences elsewhere, but
maybe we just haven't profiled carefully enough in the context of
very simple models where it might make a difference.
